item.title: Demography, Relationships and the Substitution Model
item.lead: The source links digital intimacy to demographic development via a substitution logic: if a digital alternative takes over certain functions of human relationships, behavior may shift in the long term.

blocks.text: The dossier describes the physical relationship as a trajectory involving uncertainty, investment, and potential rejection. According to the source, digital consumption offers an accessible substitute. Following this logic, a portion of the demand for physical partner relationships could decrease, with potential consequences for marriage, cohabitation, and family formation.

The text refers to Japan and South Korea as comparative examples and mentions a potential "hikikomori effect" in Europe. Here, too, the provided source does not present a elaborated empirical comparison between adult-tech consumption, relational status, and birth development. The passages function as a hypothesis and as a narrative framework.

The demographic question is particularly complex because fertility is determined by numerous factors: economy, housing costs, education, labor market, values, gender norms, health, and institutional support. Professional research must include these factors to prevent attributing a complex trend to a single digital cause.

The more defensible contribution of the dossier is therefore the question of what role digital substitutes play in a broader economy of time, attention, and relationship investment. This is a research path that can be empirically further elaborated.
